claim: An analog sensitive allele of CDK1 (cdk1F80A, called cdk1as2) was generated.
source: To investigate the role of CDK1 in regulating Baz localisation during the neuroblast cell cycle we generated an analog sensitive allele (Lopez et al., 2014) of cdk1, cdk1F80A, henceforth called cdk1as2.
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of this allele as part of the experimental approach.

claim: Control neuroblasts continued proliferating after exposure to 10 µM 1-NA-PP1.
source: While control neuroblasts continued proliferating after exposure to 1-NA-PP1, cdk1as2 neuroblasts stopped dividing (Figure 1A and A').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and A'.

claim: cdk1as2 neuroblasts stopped dividing after exposure to 10 µM 1-NA-PP1.
source: While control neuroblasts continued proliferating after exposure to 1-NA-PP1, cdk1as2 neuroblasts stopped dividing (Figure 1A and A').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and A'.

claim: Upon 1-NA-PP1 addition, early prophase cdk1as2 neuroblasts lost their apical Baz crescent and did not further proceed through mitosis.
source: Interestingly, upon 1-NA-PP1 addition, early prophase cdk1as2 neuroblasts lost their apical Baz crescent and did not further proceed through mitosis (Figure 1B), apparently reverting back to interphase, a reported effect of CDK1 inhibition (Potapova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and cited literature on CDK1 inhibition effects.

claim: Early prophase cdk1as2 neuroblasts apparently reverted back to interphase upon 1-NA-PP1 addition.
source: Interestingly, upon 1-NA-PP1 addition, early prophase cdk1as2 neuroblasts lost their apical Baz crescent and did not further proceed through mitosis (Figure 1B), apparently reverting back to interphase, a reported effect of CDK1 inhibition (Potapova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and cited literature.

claim: Reversion to interphase is a reported effect of CDK1 inhibition.
source: Interestingly, upon 1-NA-PP1 addition, early prophase cdk1as2 neuroblasts lost their apical Baz crescent and did not further proceed through mitosis (Figure 1B), apparently reverting back to interphase, a reported effect of CDK1 inhibition (Potapova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potapova et al., 2011.

claim: Mitotic slippage occurred within 10 min in the majority of cdk1as2 neuroblasts exposed to Colcemid and then 1-NA-PP1, but not in controls.
source: We first exposed neuroblasts to Colcemid to arrest them in metaphase, and then to 1-NA-PP1, which resulted in mitotic slippage within 10 min in the majority of cdk1as2 neuroblasts, but not in controls (Figure 1C and C').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and C'.

claim: Mitotic exit is an expected effect of CDK1 inhibition in metaphase-arrested cells.
source: Another expected effect of CDK1 inhibition is exit from mitosis in metaphase-arrested cells (mitotic exit; Potapova et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potapova et al., 2006.

claim: In neuroblasts that exited mitosis, Baz asymmetry was lost in a manner reminiscent of localisation changes normally occurring with the onset of anaphases of untreated neuroblasts.
source: Interestingly, in neuroblasts that exited mitosis, Baz asymmetry was lost in a manner reminiscent of localisation changes normally occurring with the onset of anaphases of untreated neuroblasts.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and comparison to normal anaphase behavior.

claim: Like in anaphase, Baz crescents spread along the lateral cortex while the cell elongated along the apico-basal axis, after which Baz eventually dissipated into the cytoplasm.
source: Like in anaphase, Baz crescents spread along the lateral cortex while the cell elongated along the apico-basal axis, after which Baz eventually dissipated into the cytoplasm (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CDK1 activity is acutely and specifically inhibited in cdk1as2 mutant flies by 10 µM of 1-NA-PP1.
source: We conclude that CDK1 activity is acutely and specifically inhibited in cdk1as2 mutant flies by 10 µM of 1-NA-PP1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing cell cycle arrest and mitotic slippage.

claim: cdk1as2 neuroblasts stopped proliferating when exposed to 1 µM or higher concentrations of 1-NA-PP1.
source: cdk1as2 neuroblasts stopped proliferating when exposed to 1 µM or higher concentrations but continued proliferating at a slower rate in the presence of 0.5 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: cdk1as2 neuroblasts continued proliferating at a slower rate in the presence of 0.5 µM 1-NA-PP1.
source: cdk1as2 neuroblasts stopped proliferating when exposed to 1 µM or higher concentrations but continued proliferating at a slower rate in the presence of 0.5 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 10 µM 1-NA-PP1 likely fully inhibits CDK1.
source: Hence, 10 µM 1-NA-PP1 likely fully inhibits CDK1 and 0.5 µM partially inhibits CDK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response data showing complete cell cycle arrest at 10 µM.

claim: 0.5 µM 1-NA-PP1 partially inhibits CDK1.
source: Hence, 10 µM 1-NA-PP1 likely fully inhibits CDK1 and 0.5 µM partially inhibits CDK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-response data showing slower proliferation at 0.5 µM.

claim: In control cells, Baz polarized in a dynamic manner, being recruited to a broad cortical crescent during prophase, which then coalesced into a smaller, brighter crescent at NEB.
source: In control cells, Baz polarized in a dynamic manner. First, it was recruited to a broad cortical crescent during prophase, which then coalesced into a smaller, brighter crescent at NEB, as previously described for unperturbed neuroblasts (Hannaford et al., 2018; Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and cited literature.

claim: Baz still polarized upon partial CDK1 inhibition in cdk1as2 neuroblasts.
source: Interestingly, although Baz still polarized upon partial CDK1 inhibition in cdk1as2 neuroblasts, apical Baz crescents appeared fainter and wider than during the previous cell cycle occurring before exposure to 1-NA-PP1 (Figure 2A and A', Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and A', Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Apical Baz crescents appeared fainter and wider upon partial CDK1 inhibition in cdk1as2 neuroblasts than during the previous cell cycle occurring before exposure to 1-NA-PP1.
source: Interestingly, although Baz still polarized upon partial CDK1 inhibition in cdk1as2 neuroblasts, apical Baz crescents appeared fainter and wider than during the previous cell cycle occurring before exposure to 1-NA-PP1 (Figure 2A and A', Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and A', Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Baz crescents fail to coalesce at NEB upon partial CDK1 inhibition.
source: Thus, Baz crescents fail to coalesce at NEB upon partial CDK1 inhibition.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that crescents are fainter and wider.

claim: Baz localisation is completely lost in dominant negative cdk1 mutant embryonic neuroblasts.
source: As Baz polarity was previously shown to be completely lost in dominant negative cdk1 mutant embryonic neuroblasts (Tio et al., 2001), we tested the effect of partial inhibition of CDK1 in larval neuroblasts in a sensitized context.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tio et al., 2001.

claim: Baz localisation is dependent on an oligomerization domain (OD) and a lipid binding domain (LD), which are functionally redundant.
source: Baz localisation is dependent on an oligomerization domain (OD) and a lipid binding domain (LD), which are functionally redundant (Kullmann and Krahn, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kullmann and Krahn, 2018.

claim: Baz deletion mutants for either the OD or LD still polarized when CDK1 was partially inhibited, and only presented an apical coalescence defect.
source: However, Baz deletion mutants for either of these domains still polarized when we partially inhibited CDK1, and only presented an apical coalescence defect (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Partial inhibition of CDK1 in embryonic neuroblasts resulted in defective coalescence but not in complete loss of polarity.
source: Again, partial inhibition of CDK1 in embryonic neuroblasts resulted in defective coalescence but not in complete loss of polarity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: High levels of CDK1 activity are needed for full apical polarization of embryonic and larval neuroblasts by driving apical coalescence.
source: We conclude that high levels of CDK1 activity are needed for full apical polarization of embryonic and larval neuroblasts by driving apical coalescence.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing coalescence defects upon partial CDK1 inhibition.

claim: The non-coalesced Baz crescents of cycling cdk1as2 neuroblasts displayed a small but significant decrease in intensity comparing two consecutive time points 75 s apart during metaphase (–9.8 ± 7.3%) upon partial CDK1 inhibition.
source: Upon partial CDK1 inhibition, we also observed that the non-coalesced Baz crescents of cycling cdk1as2 neuroblasts displayed a small but significant decrease in intensity comparing two consecutive time points 75 s apart during metaphase (–9.8 ± 7.3%), whereas Baz crescent intensity in control neuroblasts was maintained (Figure 2D and D'), suggesting a role of CDK1 in maintaining Baz polarity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and D'.

claim: Baz crescent intensity in control neuroblasts was maintained during metaphase.
source: Upon partial CDK1 inhibition, we also observed that the non-coalesced Baz crescents of cycling cdk1as2 neuroblasts displayed a small but significant decrease in intensity comparing two consecutive time points 75 s apart during metaphase (–9.8 ± 7.3%), whereas Baz crescent intensity in control neuroblasts was maintained (Figure 2D and D'), suggesting a role of CDK1 in maintaining Baz polarity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and D'.

claim: Baz crescents remained stable in metaphase-arrested cdk1as2 neuroblasts exposed to 0.5 µM 1-NA-PP1.
source: However, Baz crescents remained stable in metaphase-arrested cdk1as2 neuroblasts exposed to 0.5 µM 1-NA-PP1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 37% of metaphase-arrested neuroblasts with non-coalesced crescents gradually concentrated Baz in narrow and brighter crescents following 1-NA-PP1 washout.
source: Indeed, 37% of metaphase-arrested neuroblasts with non-coalesced crescents gradually concentrated Baz in narrow and brighter crescents following 1-NA-PP1 washout (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Partial inhibition of CDK1 can briefly destabilize Baz crescents in cycling neuroblasts, but not in metaphase-arrested neuroblasts.
source: Thus, partial inhibition of CDK1 can briefly destabilize Baz crescents in cycling neuroblasts, but not in metaphase-arrested neuroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data comparing cycling and arrested neuroblasts.

claim: NEB and Baz coalescence can be uncoupled by temporally interfering with CDK1 activity.
source: Furthermore, NEB and Baz coalescence can be uncoupled by temporally interfering with CDK1 activity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that coalescence can occur after NEB when CDK1 activity is restored.

claim: aPKC localised in dimmer apical crescents upon partial CDK1 inhibition.
source: As one key function of Baz is the recruitment of aPKC, unsurprisingly, aPKC also localised in dimmer apical crescents upon partial CDK1 inhibition (Figure 2G, I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G, I.

claim: Numb basal crescents were significantly (41 ± 51%) more intense in cdk1as2 neuroblasts compared to controls under partial CDK1 inhibition.
source: Indeed, Numb basal crescents were significantly (41 ± 51%) more intense in cdk1as2 neuroblasts compared to controls under partial CDK1 inhibition (Figure 2H and K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H and K.

claim: Miranda crescents displayed a slight, statistically insignificant increase (20 ± 49%) in intensity upon CDK1 partial inhibition.
source: Miranda crescents also displayed a slight, statistically insignificant increase (20 ± 49%) in intensity upon CDK1 partial inhibition (Figure 2G and J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and J.

claim: Partial inhibition of CDK1 prevents the coalescence of apical polarity crescents and leads to increased levels of basal fate determinants.
source: In conclusion, partial inhibition of CDK1 prevents the coalescence of apical polarity crescents and leads to increased levels of basal fate determinants (Figure 2L).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing coalescence defects and increased basal determinants.

claim: The Baz amino acid sequence contains three full consensus CDK phosphorylation sites [ST]Px[KR].
source: To determine whether the observed effects of CDK1 inhibition on Baz localisation are direct, we interrogated the Baz amino acid sequence for full consensus CDK phosphorylation sites [ST]Px[KR] (Songyang et al., 1994). We identified three phosphorylation sites, among which two have been reported to be phosphorylated in phosphoproteomic approaches in Drosophila: Serine S180 (Bodenmiller et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2008; Hilger et al., 2009) and Serine 417 (Reich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and cited literature.

claim: Serine S180 has been reported to be phosphorylated in phosphoproteomic approaches in Drosophila.
source: We identified three phosphorylation sites, among which two have been reported to be phosphorylated in phosphoproteomic approaches in Drosophila: Serine S180 (Bodenmiller et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2008; Hilger et al., 2009) and Serine 417 (Reich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bodenmiller et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2008; Hilger et al., 2009.

claim: Serine 417 has been reported to be phosphorylated in phosphoproteomic approaches in Drosophila.
source: We identified three phosphorylation sites, among which two have been reported to be phosphorylated in phosphoproteomic approaches in Drosophila: Serine S180 (Bodenmiller et al., 2008; Zhai et al., 2008; Hilger et al., 2009) and Serine 417 (Reich et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reich et al., 2019.

claim: The presence of a Cyclin-binding motif [RK]XL(X)[FYLIVMP] and of phospho-dependent Cks1-binding motifs [FILPVWY]XTP suggests the possibility of CDK regulation of Baz.
source: The presence of a Cyclin-binding motif [RK]XL(X)[FYLIVMP], (Lowe et al., 2002) and of phospho-dependent Cks1-binding motifs [FILPVWY]XTP, (McGrath et al., 2013) further suggests the possibility of CDK regulation of Baz (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and cited literature.

claim: A Baz-pS180 signal was only detected in dividing neuroblasts, and neither in interphase neuroblasts nor in neighboring neuroepithelial cells, regardless of their cell cycle stage.
source: Remarkably, a Baz-pS180 signal was only detected in dividing neuroblasts, and neither in interphase neuroblasts nor in neighboring neuroepithelial, regardless of their cell cycle stage (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Mitotic asymmetrically dividing sensory organ precursors (SOPs) were positive for Baz-pS180, whereas symmetrically dividing epidermal cells were not.
source: Again, mitotic asymmetrically dividing sensory organ precursors (SOPs) were positive for Baz-pS180, whereas symmetrically dividing epidermal cells were not (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In late L3 larval imaginal disks, dividing SOPs were positive for Baz-pS180 while symmetrically dividing columnar epithelial cells were not.
source: Similarly, in late L3 larval imaginal disks, dividing SOPs were positive for Baz-pS180 while symmetrically dividing columnar epithelial cells were not (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Cortical CyclinA colocalises with Baz-pS180 in mitotic SOPs.
source: We confirmed that cortical CyclinA colocalises with Baz-pS180 in mitotic SOPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), potentially providing a mechanism for this asymmetric cell division-specific phosphorylation event.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither Cyclin A, Cyclin B nor Cyclin B3 localised to the cortex of dividing neuroblasts.
source: However, neither Cyclin A, Cyclin B nor Cyclin B3 localised to the cortex of dividing neuroblasts, indicating that neuroblast-specific phosphorylation of Baz-S180 is not achieved through cortical Cyclin localisation in the larval brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least in the larval brain, late L3 larval imaginal discs and the pupal notum at 16 hr APF, Baz-S180 is apparently specifically phosphorylated during asymmetric cell divisions.
source: We conclude that at least in the larval brain, late L3 larval imaginal discs and the pupal notum at 16 hr APF, Baz-S180 is apparently specifically phosphorylated during asymmetric cell divisions.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing Baz-pS180 signal only in asymmetrically dividing cells.

claim: UAS-driven RNAi against RFP resulted in an apparently complete depletion of Baz::mScarlet and expected Mira localisation defects.
source: This resulted in an apparently complete depletion of Baz::mScarlet and expected Mira localisation defects (Atwood et al., 2007; Atwood and Prehoda, 2009), which were rescued by expression of our BazWT::GFP construct (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and cited literature.

claim: Expression of BazWT::GFP rescued the Mira localisation defects caused by Baz::mScarlet depletion.
source: This resulted in an apparently complete depletion of Baz::mScarlet and expected Mira localisation defects (Atwood et al., 2007; Atwood and Prehoda, 2009), which were rescued by expression of our BazWT::GFP construct (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both BazS180A::GFP and BazS180D::GFP phosphomutant constructs seemingly localised similar to BazWT::GFP throughout the cell cycle.
source: First, we examined their localisation in cycling neuroblasts and observed that both phosphomutant constructs seemingly localised similar to BazWT::GFP throughout the cell cycle (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: All Baz constructs (BazWT::GFP, BazS180A::GFP, BazS180D::GFP) were stably retained at the apical pole in metaphase-arrested neuroblasts.
source: All constructs were likewise stably retained at the apical pole in metaphase-arrested neuroblasts (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the absence of endogenous Baz, BazWT::GFP apical crescents were positive for Baz-pS180 whereas BazS180A::GFP apical crescents were not, confirming the specificity of the antibody.
source: In the absence of endogenous Baz, BazWT::GFP apical crescents were positive for Baz-pS180 whereas BazS180A::GFP apical crescents were not, confirming the specificity of the antibody (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In both BazS180A and BazS180D phosphomutants, a significant delay in the formation of basal Mira crescents was detected.
source: In both phosphomutants, we detected a significant delay in the formation of basal Mira crescents.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: Basal Mira crescents in BazS180A::GFP-expressing neuroblasts reached an equivalent cortical/cytoplasmic ratio to BazWT::GFP-expressing neuroblasts at metaphase.
source: These crescents reached an equivalent cortical/cytoplasmic ratio to BazWT::GFP-expressing neuroblasts only at metaphase in BazS180A::GFP and anaphase in BazS180D::GFP (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Basal Mira crescents in BazS180D::GFP-expressing neuroblasts reached an equivalent cortical/cytoplasmic ratio to BazWT::GFP-expressing neuroblasts at anaphase.
source: These crescents reached an equivalent cortical/cytoplasmic ratio to BazWT::GFP-expressing neuroblasts only at metaphase in BazS180A::GFP and anaphase in BazS180D::GFP (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Numb localises to basal crescents in metaphase in all BazWT::GFP-expressing, all BazS180A::GFP-expressing and most BazS180D::GFP-expressing neuroblasts.
source: Numb localises to basal crescents in metaphase in all BazWT::GFP-expressing, all BazS180A::GFP-expressing and most BazS180D::GFP-expressing neuroblasts.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: In BazS180D::GFP-expressing neuroblasts where Mira showed very low polarization (cortical/cytoplasmic ratio <2), Numb often (n=8/16 neuroblasts) localised uniformly to the cortex.
source: Interestingly, in BazS180D::GFP-expressing neuroblasts where Mira showed very low polarization (cortical/cytoplasmic ratio <2), Numb often (n=8/16 neuroblasts) localised uniformly to the cortex (Figure 4G and G').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and G'.

claim: Numb mislocalisation in metaphase was only transient as Numb localised to the basal cortex in anaphase.
source: Like for Mira, this Numb mislocalisation in metaphase was only transient as Numb localised to the basal cortex in anaphase (Figure 4H and H').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H and H'.

claim: Phosphorylation of Baz-S180 is not necessary for the coordination of Baz localisation throughout the cell cycle but is involved in the timely establishment of basal polarity in larval neuroblasts.
source: In conclusion, phosphorylation of Baz-S180 is not necessary for the coordination of Baz localisation throughout the cell cycle but is involved in the timely establishment of basal polarity in larval neuroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing delayed basal polarity in phosphomutants.

claim: The individual RNAi-mediated depletion of Baz or the Notch ligand Delta do not result in severe sensory organ formation defects.
source: The individual RNAi-mediated depletion of Baz or the Notch ligand Delta do not result in severe sensory organ formation defects.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: Co-depletion of both Baz and Delta results in a neurogenic phenotype and the near complete loss of sensory organs, indicative of a Notch loss of function.
source: However, co-depletion of both results in a neurogenic phenotype and the near complete loss of sensory organs, indicative of a Notch loss of function (Houssin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation and cited literature.

claim: Expression of Baz::GFP constructs partially rescued the formation of macrochaetes, but not that of microchaetes.
source: Expression of our Baz::GFP constructs partially rescued the formation of macrochaetes, large sensory organs formed at the beginning of pupal development, but surprisingly not that of microchaetes, smaller sensory organs formed later during pupal development (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significantly more macrochaete bristles formed when expressing either BazS180A or BazS180D phosphomutant compared to the rescue with BazWT::GFP.
source: We observed that significantly more macrochaete bristles formed when expressing either phosphomutant compared to the rescue with BazWT::GFP (Figure 5D and D').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and D'.

claim: Rescue by the Baz-S180 phosphomutants in the baz, delta double RNAi background resulted in significantly more SOPs to be formed.
source: Rescue by the Baz-S180 phosphomutants in the baz, delta double RNAi background resulted in significantly more SOPs to be formed (Figure 5F) and in significantly more socket-to-shaft transformations (Figure 5G) than rescue by BazWT::GFP, suggesting a Notch loss of function during lateral inhibition and following asymmetric cell divisions, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Rescue by the Baz-S180 phosphomutants in the baz, delta double RNAi background resulted in significantly more socket-to-shaft transformations.
source: Rescue by the Baz-S180 phosphomutants in the baz, delta double RNAi background resulted in significantly more SOPs to be formed (Figure 5F) and in significantly more socket-to-shaft transformations (Figure 5G) than rescue by BazWT::GFP, suggesting a Notch loss of function during lateral inhibition and following asymmetric cell divisions, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In the absence of Delta, phosphorylation of Baz-S180 affects sensory organ formation both during the initial specification of SOPs and during the asymmetric cell divisions they undergo later.
source: Thus, in the absence of Delta, phosphorylation of Baz-S180 affects sensory organ formation both during the initial specification of SOPs and during the asymmetric cell divisions they undergo later.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing effects on SOP specification and socket-to-shaft transformations.

claim: Patches of Baz-pS180-positive cells overlapped with Delta-positive stripes at 8 hr APF.
source: We observed patches of Baz-pS180-positive cells that overlapped with these Delta-positive stripes at 8 hr APF (Figure 5H)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: A strong Baz-pS180 signal was present outside of Delta-positive stripes at 8 hr APF, in particular close to the scutellar macrochaetes, in a region devoid of microchaete SOPs.
source: Importantly, a strong Baz-pS180 signal was also present outside of these stripes, in particular close to the scutellar macrochaetes (Figure 5H, arrowhead), in a region devoid of microchaete SOPs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Baz-S180 phosphorylation may have additional roles during development beyond asymmetric cell division.
source: This suggests that Baz-S180 phosphorylation may have additional roles during development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Baz-pS180 signal outside of regions with asymmetric cell divisions.

claim: Only a subset of microchaete SOPs in the pupal notum expressed Neur-GAL4, UASz-controlled Baz::GFP constructs.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that only a subset of microchaete SOPs in the pupal notum expressed our Neur-GAL4, UASz-controlled Baz::GFP constructs (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Baz-S180 phosphomutants localisation did not appear to be affected during the ACD of pI.
source: The Baz-S180 phosphomutants localisation did not appear to be affected during the ACD of pI: in metaphase, they formed posterior crescents which intensity was not significantly different from BazWT::GFP (Figure 6D and D').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and D'.

claim: In contrast to pI division, the Baz-S180 phosphomutants localisation differed from BazWT::GFP during pIIa metaphase.
source: In contrast to pI division, the Baz-S180 phosphomutants localisation differed from BazWT::GFP during pIIa metaphase.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: BazS180A::GFP formed posterior crescents during pIIa metaphase, but with a significantly weaker cortical-to-cytoplasmic ratio than BazWT::GFP.
source: Like BazWT::GFP, BazS180A::GFP formed posterior crescents, but with a significantly weaker cortical-to-cytoplasmic ratio.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: BazS180D::GFP crescents appeared enlarged and displaced toward the anterior pole during pIIa metaphase, leading to a significant increase of the anterior cortical signal.
source: BazS180D::GFP crescents appeared enlarged and displaced toward the anterior pole, leading to a significant increase of the anterior cortical signal (Figure 6E and E').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and E'.

claim: Baz localisation during the ACD of pIIa but not its mother cell pI is regulated by Baz-S180 phosphorylation.
source: Therefore, Baz localisation during the ACD of pIIa but not its mother cell pI is regulated by Baz-S180 phosphorylation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing differential effects in pI vs pIIa.

claim: Baz-positive puncta were present at the basolateral pIIb/pIIa interface whether Baz::GFP was expressed only in pIIb or pIIa.
source: Baz-positive puncta were present at the basolateral pIIb/pIIa interface whether Baz::GFP was expressed only in pIIb (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) or pIIa (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and 1F.

claim: Baz::GFP only localised to the cortical patch forming during pIIa division when it was expressed in pIIb.
source: In contrast, Baz::GFP only localised to the cortical patch forming during pIIa division when it was expressed in pIIb (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: pIIb and pIIa both contribute to basolateral Baz nanocluster.
source: Thus, pIIb and pIIa both contribute to basolateral Baz nanocluster (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, arrows), whereas the Baz present at the cortical patch during pIIa division is exclusively present in pIIIb (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, arrowhead).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing Baz presence in both cell types.

claim: The Baz present at the cortical patch during pIIa division is exclusively present in pIIIb.
source: Thus, pIIb and pIIa both contribute to basolateral Baz nanocluster (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, arrows), whereas the Baz present at the cortical patch during pIIa division is exclusively present in pIIIb (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, arrowhead).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing Baz presence only when expressed in pIIb.

claim: pIIb divides perpendicularly to the plane of the epithelium.
source: Unlike the pI and pIIa cells which orient their divisions within the plane of the epithelium, pIIb divides perpendicularly to the plane of the epithelium (Gho et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gho et al., 1999.

claim: pIIb tended to divide perpendicularly to the plane of the epithelium in most cases where Baz::GFP was present in both pIIb and pIIa.
source: We observed that pIIb also tended to do so in most cases where Baz::GFP was present in both pIIb and pIIa.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: When Baz::GFP was present in pIIb but not in pIIa, pIIb tended to divide within the plane of the epithelium.
source: Surprisingly, when Baz::GFP was present in pIIb but not in pIIa, pIIb tended to divide within the plane of the epithelium (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I.

claim: The orientation of the pIIb division is controlled in a cell non-autonomous manner by the levels of Baz in its sister cell pIIa.
source: Thus, the orientation of the pIIb division is controlled in a cell non-autonomous manner by the levels of Baz in its sister cell pIIa.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing pIIb division orientation depends on Baz expression in pIIa.

claim: Incubation of Baz2-320 with CDK1/CyclinB1 resulted in a large increase of anti-Baz-pS180 binding.
source: Indeed, although the phospho-specific Baz-PS180 slightly bound to Baz2-320 in the absence of CDK1/CyclinB1 or ATP, incubation with CDK1/CyclinB1 resulted in a large increase of anti-Baz-pS180 binding (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CDK1 phosphorylates Baz-S180 in vitro.
source: We conclude from these results that CDK1 phosphorylates Baz-S180 in vitro.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the western blot and mass spectrometry data.

claim: A full consensus CDK phosphosite (S187) was identified on PARD3 in close proximity to a 14-3-3 binding site, like S180 in Baz.
source: Interestingly, although the sequence of the disordered region surrounding S180 does not appear to be conserved in the Baz human ortholog PARD3, we identified on PARD3 a full consensus CDK phosphosite (S187) in close proximity, like S180 in Baz, to a 14-3-3 binding site (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: PARD3-S187 was previously found phosphorylated in high-throughput mass spectrometry studies.
source: PARD3-S187 was previously found phosphorylated in high-throughput mass spectrometry studies (Lin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lin et al., 2021.

claim: PARD3-S187 was only phosphorylated in the presence of CDK1/CyclinB1 complexes.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we observed that PARD3-S187 was only phosphorylated in the presence of CDK1/CyclinB1 complexes, along with a few other residues not matching consensus CDK phosphosites (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: CDK1 phosphorylates human PARD3 in vitro on a Serine which localisation closely matches Baz-S180.
source: Thus, CDK1 phosphorylates human PARD3 in vitro on a Serine which localisation closely matches Baz-S180.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mass spectrometry data showing PARD3-S187 phosphorylation.

claim: Dominant negative or thermosensitive cdk1 alleles do not prevent embryonic neuroblasts from cycling but disrupt their polarity.
source: Based on the observation on fixed tissues that dominant negative or thermosensitive cdk1 alleles do not prevent embryonic neuroblasts from cycling but disrupt their polarity, asymmetric cell division was proposed to strictly rely on high levels of CDK1 activity (Tio et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tio et al., 2001.

claim: Asymmetric cell division was proposed to strictly rely on high levels of CDK1 activity.
source: Based on the observation on fixed tissues that dominant negative or thermosensitive cdk1 alleles do not prevent embryonic neuroblasts from cycling but disrupt their polarity, asymmetric cell division was proposed to strictly rely on high levels of CDK1 activity (Tio et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tio et al., 2001.

claim: Loss of Baz polarity was previously only reported with the dominant negative cdk1E51Q allele.
source: A possible cause for this discrepancy could be that loss of Baz polarity was previously only reported with the dominant negative cdk1E51Q allele, for which neomorphic activity cannot be ruled out, whereas loss of polarity in the thermosensitive cdk1 genetic situation was only reported for another apical polarity protein, Inscuteable.
evidence: This is based on review of previous literature.

claim: Baz functions upstream of Inscuteable.
source: Considering that Baz functions upstream of Inscuteable (Schober et al., 1999), it is possible that Baz localisation is not affected in this situation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schober et al., 1999.

claim: aPKC inhibition can result in apical crescents coalescing in the wrong direction.
source: Our previous observation that aPKC inhibition can result in apical crescents coalescing in the wrong direction (Hannaford et al., 2019) suggests that apical polarity proteins are involved in some aspects of this process.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hannaford et al., 2019.

claim: Apical coalescence of neuroblasts is driven by basal-to-apical actomyosin-driven cortical flows.
source: RhoGAPs and RhoGEFs are promising candidates for this: first, apical coalescence of neuroblasts is driven by basal-to-apical actomyosin-driven cortical flows (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), reminiscent of the ones polarising C. elegans embryos (Munro et al., 2004) induced by asymmetric localisation of the RhoGEF ECT-2 (Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006) second, ECT-2 can be phosphorylated by CDK1 (Niiya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oon and Prehoda, 2019.

claim: Cortical flows polarising C. elegans embryos are induced by asymmetric localisation of the RhoGEF ECT-2.
source: RhoGAPs and RhoGEFs are promising candidates for this: first, apical coalescence of neuroblasts is driven by basal-to-apical actomyosin-driven cortical flows (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), reminiscent of the ones polarising C. elegans embryos (Munro et al., 2004) induced by asymmetric localisation of the RhoGEF ECT-2 (Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006) second, ECT-2 can be phosphorylated by CDK1 (Niiya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Munro et al., 2004 and Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006.

claim: ECT-2 can be phosphorylated by CDK1.
source: RhoGAPs and RhoGEFs are promising candidates for this: first, apical coalescence of neuroblasts is driven by basal-to-apical actomyosin-driven cortical flows (Oon and Prehoda, 2019), reminiscent of the ones polarising C. elegans embryos (Munro et al., 2004) induced by asymmetric localisation of the RhoGEF ECT-2 (Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006) second, ECT-2 can be phosphorylated by CDK1 (Niiya et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niiya et al., 2005.

claim: Enlarged Baz crescents were observed in aurora A mutants.
source: Interestingly, enlarged Baz crescents were observed in aurora A mutants (Wang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2006.

claim: CDK1 activates Aurora A.
source: Given that CDK1 activates Aurora A (Van Horn et al., 2010), this raises the possibility that CDK1 drives apical coalescence via Aurora A activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Van Horn et al., 2010.

claim: Baz localisation is dependent on an oligomerization domain (OD) and a lipid binding domain (LD), which are functionally redundant.
source: Baz localisation is dependent on an oligomerization domain (OD) and a lipid binding domain (LD), which are functionally redundant (Kullmann and Krahn, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kullmann and Krahn, 2018.

claim: Baz functions redundantly with the polarity protein PAR-6 in tracheal terminal cells branching.
source: Accordingly, Baz functions redundantly with the polarity protein PAR-6 in tracheal terminal cells branching (Jones and Metzstein, 2011), with the transmembrane protein Crumbs in the maintenance of epithelial polarity (Müller and Wieschaus, 1996), with the Notch ligand Delta in the formation of sensory organs (Houssin et al., 2021), and with the apical polarity Pins in the generation of size asymmetry during neuroblasts asymmetric cell division (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jones and Metzstein, 2011.

claim: Baz functions redundantly with the transmembrane protein Crumbs in the maintenance of epithelial polarity.
source: Accordingly, Baz functions redundantly with the polarity protein PAR-6 in tracheal terminal cells branching (Jones and Metzstein, 2011), with the transmembrane protein Crumbs in the maintenance of epithelial polarity (Müller and Wieschaus, 1996), with the Notch ligand Delta in the formation of sensory organs (Houssin et al., 2021), and with the apical polarity Pins in the generation of size asymmetry during neuroblasts asymmetric cell division (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller and Wieschaus, 1996.

claim: Baz functions redundantly with the Notch ligand Delta in the formation of sensory organs.
source: Accordingly, Baz functions redundantly with the polarity protein PAR-6 in tracheal terminal cells branching (Jones and Metzstein, 2011), with the transmembrane protein Crumbs in the maintenance of epithelial polarity (Müller and Wieschaus, 1996), with the Notch ligand Delta in the formation of sensory organs (Houssin et al., 2021), and with the apical polarity Pins in the generation of size asymmetry during neuroblasts asymmetric cell division (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Houssin et al., 2021.

claim: Baz functions redundantly with the apical polarity protein Pins in the generation of size asymmetry during neuroblasts asymmetric cell division.
source: Accordingly, Baz functions redundantly with the polarity protein PAR-6 in tracheal terminal cells branching (Jones and Metzstein, 2011), with the transmembrane protein Crumbs in the maintenance of epithelial polarity (Müller and Wieschaus, 1996), with the Notch ligand Delta in the formation of sensory organs (Houssin et al., 2021), and with the apical polarity Pins in the generation of size asymmetry during neuroblasts asymmetric cell division (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2003.

claim: The robustness of Baz function relies on a lipid binding domain and an oligomerization domain, which are both sufficient on their own to support Baz localisation and function.
source: Beyond redundancies with other proteins, the robustness of Baz function relies on a lipid binding domain and an oligomerization domain, which are both sufficient on their own to support Baz localisation and function (Kullmann and Krahn, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kullmann and Krahn, 2018.

claim: Pins is known to function redundantly with Baz in neuroblasts.
source: A very likely candidate for this is Pins, known to function redundantly with Baz in neuroblasts (Cai et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2000; Izumi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2003; Yu et al., 2000; Izumi et al., 2004.

claim: The generation of distinct cell fates during development depends on asymmetric cell division of progenitor cells.
source: The generation of distinct cell fates during development depends on asymmetric cell division of progenitor cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about developmental biology.

claim: In the central and peripheral nervous system of Drosophila, progenitor cells respectively called neuroblasts or sensory organ precursors use PAR polarity during mitosis to control cell fate determination in their daughter cells.
source: In the central and peripheral nervous system of Drosophila, progenitor cells respectively called neuroblasts or sensory organ precursors use PAR polarity during mitosis to control cell fate determination in their daughter cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: How polarity and the cell cycle are coupled, and how the cell cycle machinery regulates PAR protein function and cell fate determination is poorly understood.
source: How polarity and the cell cycle are coupled, and how the cell cycle machinery regulates PAR protein function and cell fate determination is poorly understood.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Bazooka is the Drosophila homolog of PAR-3.
source: We describe a novel in vivo phosphorylation of Bazooka, the Drosophila homolog of PAR-3, on Serine180, a consensus CDK phosphorylation site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein homology.

claim: Cell fate differences in daughter cells can stem from the asymmetric subcellular localisation of fate determinants in the dividing cell.
source: Cell fate differences in the resulting daughter cells can stem, for instance, from the asymmetric subcellular localisation of fate determinants in the dividing cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about asymmetric cell division.

claim: The conserved PAR polarity complex is composed of PAR-3, PAR-6 and atypical protein kinase C (aPKC).
source: In many asymmetric dividing cells, the conserved PAR polarity complex, composed of PAR-3, PAR-6 and atypical protein kinase C (aPKC) (Goldstein and Macara, 2007; Goehring, 2014), polarises prior to division.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldstein and Macara, 2007; Goehring, 2014.

claim: The PAR polarity complex exhibits cell-cycle dependent localisation in the C. elegans zygote.
source: The PAR polarity complex exhibits cell-cycle dependent localisation in the C. elegans zygote (Kemphues, 2000) and many stem and precursor cells, such as neural precursors in the chick (Das and Storey, 2012) and fish (Alexandre et al., 2010), muscle stem cells in the mouse (Dumont et al., 2015), and stem and precursor cells of the developing central and peripheral nervous system of Drosophila (Wodarz et al., 1999; Schober et al., 1999; Bellaïche et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kemphues, 2000.

claim: Cell cycle kinases like Plk1 and Aurora A regulate polarity in the C. elegans zygote required for the establishment of PAR anterior-posterior polarisation.
source: Cell cycle kinases like Plk1 and Aurora A (Kim and Griffin, 2020; Reich et al., 2019; Schumacher et al., 1998) regulate polarity in the zygote required for the establishment of PAR anterior-posterior polarisation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim and Griffin, 2020; Reich et al., 2019; Schumacher et al., 1998.

claim: The homologs of Plk1 and Aurora A and the master regulator of cell cycle transitions, CDK1, have been implicated in linking cell cycle and asymmetric division in the central and peripheral nervous system of flies.
source: In flies, the homologs of Plk1 and Aurora A and the master regulator of cell cycle transitions, CDK1 (Nurse, 1997), have been implicated in linking cell cycle and asymmetric division in the central and peripheral nervous system (Tio et al., 2001; Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tio et al., 2001; Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007.

claim: CDK1 is the master regulator of cell cycle transitions.
source: In flies, the homologs of Plk1 and Aurora A and the master regulator of cell cycle transitions, CDK1 (Nurse, 1997), have been implicated in linking cell cycle and asymmetric division in the central and peripheral nervous system (Tio et al., 2001; Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nurse, 1997.

claim: Drosophila neural stem cells called neuroblasts are a well-studied model for asymmetric cell division.
source: Drosophila neural stem cells called neuroblasts are a well-studied model for asymmetric cell division (Sunchu and Cabernard, 2020; Tassan and Kubiak, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sunchu and Cabernard, 2020; Tassan and Kubiak, 2017.

claim: Neuroblasts divide asymmetrically generating a self-renewed neuroblast and a differentiating daughter cell.
source: Neuroblasts divide asymmetrically generating a self-renewed neuroblast and a differentiating daughter cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroblast division.

claim: In prophase, PAR proteins (PAR-6, aPKC and PAR-3, known as Baz in Drosophila) accumulate to a cortical domain, defining the apical pole.
source: In prophase, PAR proteins (PAR-6, aPKC and PAR-3, known as Baz in Drosophila) accumulate to a cortical domain, defining the apical pole (Rolls et al., 2003; Wodarz et al., 1999; Wodarz et al., 2000; Petronczki and Knoblich, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rolls et al., 2003; Wodarz et al., 1999; Wodarz et al., 2000; Petronczki and Knoblich, 2001.

claim: The earliest signs of neuroblast polarisation in mitosis include the recruitment of Baz from the cytoplasm to a broad apical area at the onset of prophase.
source: The earliest signs of neuroblast polarisation in mitosis include the recruitment of Baz from the cytoplasm to a broad apical area at the onset of prophase (Hannaford et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hannaford et al., 2018.

claim: At nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB), basal-to-apical actin-driven cortical flows lead to the coalescence of Baz into a continuous cluster that forms a bright apical crescent.
source: At nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB), basal-to-apical actin-driven cortical flows then lead to the coalescence of Baz into continuous a continuous cluster that forms a bright apical crescent (Oon and Prehoda, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oon and Prehoda, 2019.

claim: The signals that drive Baz coalescence and its functional significance in neuroblasts are unknown.
source: The signals that drive Baz coalescence and its functional significance in neuroblasts are unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Following nuclear envelope break down, the PAR complex excludes cell fate determinants such as Miranda, Pon and Numb from the apical pole via aPKC activity, leading to their localisation at the opposite basal pole.
source: Following nuclear envelope break down, the PAR complex excludes cell fate determinants such as Miranda, Pon and Numb from the apical pole via aPKC activity, leading to their localisation at the opposite basal pole.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuroblast polarity.

claim: At metaphase, the mitotic spindle aligns with the apical basal polarity axis, leading to the asymmetric segregation of fate determinants into the differentiating daughter cell.
source: At metaphase, the mitotic spindle aligns with the apical basal polarity axis, leading to the asymmetric segregation of fate determinants into the differentiating daughter cell (Gillies and Cabernard, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gillies and Cabernard, 2011.

claim: Cell polarity and the cell cycle are tightly coordinated in neuroblasts, with apical polarity assembled and disassembled at each cell cycle.
source: Therefore, cell polarity and the cell cycle are tightly coordinated in neuroblasts, with apical polarity assembled and disassembled at each cell cycle.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on established knowledge.

claim: Baz is heavily regulated by phosphorylation by different kinases including PAR-1 and aPKC in flies.
source: Baz is heavily regulated by phosphorylation by different kinases including PAR-1 and aPKC in flies (Benton and St Johnston, 2003; Morais-de-Sá et al., 2010) and additionally by Aurora A, Plk1 and other kinases in other systems (Dickinson et al., 2017; Khazaei and Püschel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benton and St Johnston, 2003; Morais-de-Sá et al., 2010.

claim: Baz is additionally regulated by phosphorylation by Aurora A, Plk1 and other kinases in other systems.
source: Baz is heavily regulated by phosphorylation by different kinases including PAR-1 and aPKC in flies (Benton and St Johnston, 2003; Morais-de-Sá et al., 2010) and additionally by Aurora A, Plk1 and other kinases in other systems (Dickinson et al., 2017; Khazaei and Püschel, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dickinson et al., 2017; Khazaei and Püschel, 2009.

claim: Aurora A phosphorylates PAR-6.
source: Some polarity proteins are phosphorylated by cell-cycle-dependent kinases during asymmetric neuroblast division: Aurora A phosphorylates PAR-6 (Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008) and Polo, the fly homolog of Plk1, phosphorylates Pon (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008.

claim: Polo, the fly homolog of Plk1, phosphorylates Pon.
source: Some polarity proteins are phosphorylated by cell-cycle-dependent kinases during asymmetric neuroblast division: Aurora A phosphorylates PAR-6 (Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008) and Polo, the fly homolog of Plk1, phosphorylates Pon (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2007.

claim: Apical Baz polarity remains largely unaffected in aurora A and polo mutants.
source: Importantly, although these phosphorylation events control basal polarity, apical Baz polarity remains largely unaffected in aurora A and polo mutants (Lee et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007.

claim: Baz asymmetric localisation was reported to be lost in embryonic neuroblasts expressing a dominant negative form of CDK1.
source: Interestingly, Baz asymmetric localisation was reported to be lost in embryonic neuroblasts expressing a dominant negative form of CDK1 (Tio et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tio et al., 2001.

claim: Baz polarity is coupled to the cell cycle in asymmetrically dividing sensory organ precursors (SOPs) in the peripheral nervous system of the fly.
source: Like in neuroblasts, Baz polarity is coupled to the cell cycle in asymmetrically dividing sensory organ precursors (SOPs) in the peripheral nervous system of the fly (Bellaïche et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellaïche et al., 2001.

claim: SOP cells are first specified through a Notch-dependent lateral inhibition mechanism.
source: In this system, SOP cells are first specified through a Notch-dependent lateral inhibition mechanism (Simpson, 1990), and then undergo a series of asymmetric cell divisions generating five cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simpson, 1990.

claim: At the end of each SOP division, the asymmetric segregation of Notch regulators results in the differential activation of the Notch pathway in each daughter cell, assigning them different identities.
source: At the end of each division, the asymmetric segregation of Notch regulators results in the differential activation of the Notch pathway in each daughter cell, assigning them different identities (Schweisguth, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schweisguth, 2015.

claim: Downregulation of CDK1 activity in SOPs delays mitosis and causes mother-to-daughter cell fate transformations occurring without divisions, affecting polarity orientation when cells eventually divide, and ultimately leads to loss of external organs.
source: Downregulation of CDK1 activity in SOPs delays mitosis and causes mother-to-daughter cell fate transformations occurring without divisions, affecting polarity orientation when cells eventually divide, and ultimately leads to loss of external organs (Fichelson and Gho, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fichelson and Gho, 2004.

claim: Cyclin A was recently found to colocalise with Baz at the posterior cortex of mitotic SOPs.
source: Interestingly, Cyclin A, a CDK1 activator, was recently found to colocalise with Baz at the posterior cortex of mitotic SOPs (Darnat et al., 2022), consistent with the possibility that CDK1 may directly phosphorylate Baz.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darnat et al., 2022.
